paragraphs.heading: A fraction made of polynomials
paragraphs.text: A rational function is a function you can write as a fraction whose top and bottom are both polynomials. We usually call them P and Q, with P on top, Q underneath, and Q not allowed to be the zero function. The function only makes sense where the bottom is not zero, so its domain, the set of inputs it accepts, is every x for which Q(x) is not zero.

paragraphs.heading: What counts and what does not
paragraphs.text: A constant such as f(x) = π is a rational function, because a constant is a polynomial. That holds even though every output it gives is an irrational number. Every polynomial P(x) also qualifies: just put Q(x) = 1 underneath. A function like sin(x), which cannot be written as such a fraction, is not rational, though nobody usually calls it irrational.

paragraphs.heading: Combining and simplifying
paragraphs.text: Add, multiply or divide two rational functions, as long as you never divide by the zero polynomial, and the result is again a rational function. Simplifying takes care. The function x/x equals 1 for every x except 0, where it has a gap called a removable singularity, and tidying the fraction into standard form can quietly erase such gaps. One way around this is to treat A(x)/B(x) and C(x)/D(x) as the same thing whenever A(x)D(x) = B(x)C(x). Under that rule, x/x and 1/1 are simply equivalent.

paragraphs.heading: Proper functions and degree
paragraphs.text: A rational function is called proper when P has a lower degree than Q and both are real polynomials, a name borrowed from proper fractions among the rational numbers. The word degree itself is slippery here: there are several definitions that do not agree. In asymptotic analysis, for instance, the degree is the numerator's degree minus the denominator's. In network analysis, a ratio of two polynomials of degree at most two often goes by the name biquadratic function.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the real numbers
paragraphs.text: The coefficients need not be rational numbers; they can come from any field K. With complex coefficients, the domain becomes the complex numbers z for which Q(z) ≠ 0. Every rational function extends naturally to the whole Riemann sphere, and applying one over and over there forms a discrete dynamical system. A complex rational function of degree one is called a Möbius transformation.

paragraphs.heading: A family of their own
paragraphs.text: All the rational functions over a field K together form a field too: the field of fractions built from the polynomial functions over K. In abstract algebra, the field of rational expressions over a field F is written F(X). A rational expression can be written as P/Q in more than one way, but there is exactly one way with P and Q of lowest degree and Q monic. That mirrors how a fraction of whole numbers has one form in lowest terms once common factors are cancelled.

paragraphs.heading: Solving number patterns
paragraphs.text: Rational functions are a tool for sequences. If you expand one as a Taylor series, its coefficients follow a linear recurrence relation, and any sequence that obeys such a recurrence, used as Taylor coefficients, gives back a rational function. To get an explicit formula for the terms, split a proper rational function by partial fractions into pieces of the form 1 / (ax + b), then expand each piece as a geometric series. This is the method of generating functions.
